lines.say: At the end of a long day at the computer, can you say how many hours you really worked?
Most of us can't. We remember being busy, but not the twenty minutes on YouTube, or the quick Instagram check that turned into an hour.
In this video, I'll show you FocusLens, a free app that tracks where your screen time goes. And I'll explain exactly how it works inside.

scenes.heading: What is [[FocusLens]]?
items: A **tracker** that notes which app or website is in front of you, **every second**
A **dashboard** in your browser that turns it into **time, scores and habits**
**Free and private**: plain Python, no account, data never leaves your PC

lines.say: So, what is FocusLens?
Think of it as a fitness tracker, but for your attention. A small program runs in the background and notes which app or website is in front of you, every second.
Then a dashboard in your browser turns that data into time, scores, and habits.
It's plain Python with no extra packages and no account. And your data never leaves your computer.

lines.say: Under the hood, it works in four stages.
First, capture. Every second, it asks Windows which window is active, and how long since you last clicked or typed.
Second, classify. Rules turn a program and a tab title into a named activity, like YouTube, and a category: productive, neutral, or distracting.
Third, analyze. The sessions become a focus score, deep-work blocks, and the habit loops that cost you time.
And fourth, show it all on a dashboard that only your own computer can open.

**3h 5m** productive · **43m** lost

lines.say: Without tracking, all you have is a feeling. I worked all day. But the hours are a blur, and distractions always feel shorter than they were.
With FocusLens, you get facts: exact productive time, exact lost time, and the specific habits behind them. And you can't improve what you don't measure.
Here's the dashboard. This is demo data, so you can see a full day.
Top left is your focus score, from zero to a hundred. It measures how much of your screen time went into real work.
Next to it: total screen time, productive time against your daily goal, and time lost to distractions, each compared with your seven-day average.
The day timeline shows every minute, colored by category. The purple bars underneath are deep-work blocks: twenty-five minutes or more of focused work.
And on the right, the coach turns your numbers into advice: your best focus hour, your biggest time sink, and habit loops.
Further down, every app and website is listed with the exact time you spent on it, and how many separate sessions.
Open one, and you see the window titles behind it. Here, the exact GitHub page I was on.
If something is in the wrong category, change it right here. Every day, past and present, is recalculated instantly.
Then the trends: productive time versus lost time, day by day, with the focus score above each bar.
This heatmap is my favorite part. Each square is one hour of one weekday, over the last four weeks. The redder it is, the more time you usually lose there.
And these are your triggers: what you open right after working. After VS Code, X. After the terminal, YouTube. Once you see the loop, you can break it.

lines.say: Let's walk through the four parts that matter.
Step one is the tracker, in tracker dot py.

do.text:
"""Foreground-window tracker for Windows (stdlib only, uses ctypes).

Every second it samples the active window (process + title) and the time since
the last keyboard/mouse input. Consecutive identical samples are merged into one
session row in SQLite, so the database stays small.
"""
import ctypes
import ctypes.wintypes as wt
import os
import threading
import time

import storage
import rules

user32 = ctypes.WinDLL("user32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)

PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION = 0x1000


class LASTINPUTINFO(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [("cbSize", wt.UINT), ("dwTime", wt.DWORD)]


user32.GetForegroundWindow.restype = wt.HWND
user32.GetWindowTextLengthW.argtypes = [wt.HWND]
user32.GetWindowTextW.argtypes = [wt.HWND, wt.LPWSTR, ctypes.c_int]
user32.GetWindowThreadProcessId.argtypes = [wt.HWND, ctypes.POINTER(wt.DWORD)]
kernel32.OpenProcess.restype = wt.HANDLE
kernel32.QueryFullProcessImageNameW.argtypes = [wt.HANDLE, wt.DWORD, wt.LPWSTR, ctypes.POINTER(wt.DWORD)]
kernel32.GetTickCount.restype = wt.DWORD


def idle_seconds():
    info = LASTINPUTINFO()
    info.cbSize = ctypes.sizeof(LASTINPUTINFO)
    if not user32.GetLastInputInfo(ctypes.byref(info)):
        return 0.0
    elapsed = (kernel32.GetTickCount() - info.dwTime) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return elapsed / 1000.0


def foreground_window():
    """Return (exe_name, window_title) of the active window, or (None, None)."""
    hwnd = user32.GetForegroundWindow()
    if not hwnd:
        return None, None
    length = user32.GetWindowTextLengthW(hwnd)
    buf = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(length + 1)
    user32.GetWindowTextW(hwnd, buf, length + 1)
    title = buf.value

    pid = wt.DWORD()
    user32.GetWindowThreadProcessId(hwnd, ctypes.byref(pid))
    exe = None
    handle = kernel32.OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, False, pid.value)
    if handle:
        try:
            size = wt.DWORD(1024)
            path = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(size.value)
            if kernel32.QueryFullProcessImageNameW(handle, 0, path, ctypes.byref(size)):
                exe = os.path.basename(path.value).lower()
        finally:
            kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    return exe, title


class Tracker(threading.Thread):
    SAMPLE_EVERY = 1.0
    FLUSH_EVERY = 10.0

    def __init__(self, db_path):
        super().__init__(daemon=True)
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._stop = threading.Event()

    def stop(self):
        self._stop.set()

    def _sample(self, cfg):
        """Return (exe, title, started_at) for the current state."""
        now = time.time()
        exe, title = foreground_window()
        idle = idle_seconds()
        threshold = cfg["settings"]["idle_minutes"] * 60
        # Watching a video produces no input; give media a longer grace period.
        if exe and rules.is_media(exe, title or "", cfg):
            threshold = max(threshold, cfg["settings"]["media_idle_minutes"] * 60)
        if exe in (None, "lockapp.exe", "logonui.exe") or idle >= threshold:
            return storage.IDLE, "", now - (idle if idle >= threshold else 0)
        return exe, title or "", now

    def run(self):
        conn = storage.connect(self.db_path)
        cfg = rules.load_config()
        cfg_loaded = time.time()
        current = None  # dict(id, exe, title, end)
        last_flush = 0.0
        while not self._stop.is_set():
            try:
                if time.time() - cfg_loaded > 30:
                    cfg, cfg_loaded = rules.load_config(), time.time()
                exe, title, started = self._sample(cfg)
                now = time.time()
                # A sleep/hibernate gap: close the old row where it really ended.
                if current and now - current["end"] > 30:
                    storage.update_end(conn, current["id"], current["end"])
                    current = None
                if current and current["exe"] == exe and current["title"] == title:
                    current["end"] = now
                    if now - last_flush >= self.FLUSH_EVERY:
                        storage.update_end(conn, current["id"], now)
                        last_flush = now
                else:
                    start = now
                    if current:
                        # When going idle, the idle period began at the last input.
                        start = max(min(started, now), current.get("start", started))
                        storage.update_end(conn, current["id"], start)
                    row_id = storage.insert(conn, start, now, exe, title)
                    current = {"id": row_id, "exe": exe, "title": title, "start": start, "end": now}
                    last_flush = now
            except Exception as exc:  # never let the tracker die
                print("tracker error:", exc)
            self._stop.wait(self.SAMPLE_EVERY)
        if current:
            storage.update_end(conn, current["id"], time.time())
        conn.close()

lines.say: Windows can tell any program which window is in front. Python's built-in ctypes module lets us ask, without installing anything.
lines.tts: Windows can tell any program which window is in front. Python's built-in C types module lets us ask, without installing anything.

lines.say: This function returns two clues: the program's file name, like chrome dot exe, and the window title, which for a browser is the name of the tab.
The third clue is idle time: the seconds since your last mouse move or key press.
After three minutes without input, you're marked as away. But while a video plays, it waits thirty minutes, because watching doesn't need clicks.

do.label: Videos get a longer grace period

lines.say: Every second, the loop compares the new sample with the current one. If nothing changed, it just extends the session. So an hour in one app is one database row, not thirty-six hundred.
Step two: turning raw data into names. That's rules dot py.

"""Turns a raw (exe, window title) into a named activity and a category.

Categories: productive, neutral, distracting. Everything is editable in
config.json (created on first run) or from the dashboard.
"""
import copy
import json
import os
import sys
import threading

BASE = os.path.dirname(sys.executable if getattr(sys, "frozen", False) else os.path.abspath(__file__))
CONFIG_PATH = os.path.join(BASE, "config.json")
CATEGORIES = ("productive", "neutral", "distracting")
_lock = threading.Lock()

BROWSERS = {
    "chrome.exe": "Google Chrome", "msedge.exe": "Microsoft Edge", "firefox.exe": "Firefox",
    "brave.exe": "Brave", "opera.exe": "Opera", "opera_gx.exe": "Opera GX",
    "vivaldi.exe": "Vivaldi", "arc.exe": "Arc", "iexplore.exe": "Internet Explorer",
}

DEFAULT_CONFIG = {
    "settings": {
        "goal_hours": 6,            # daily productive-time goal
        "idle_minutes": 3,          # no input for this long = away
        "media_idle_minutes": 30,   # grace period while a video is playing
    },
    # exe -> [display name, category]
    "apps": {
        "code.exe": ["VS Code", "productive"],
        "cursor.exe": ["Cursor", "productive"],
        "devenv.exe": ["Visual Studio", "productive"],

        "teams.exe": ["Teams", "neutral"],

        {"name": "TikTok", "keywords": ["tiktok"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "X / Twitter", "keywords": ["twitter", " / x"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "Reddit", "keywords": ["reddit"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "Pinterest", "keywords": ["pinterest"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "Snapchat", "keywords": ["snapchat"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "WhatsApp Web", "keywords": ["whatsapp"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "Messenger", "keywords": ["messenger"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "Online shopping", "keywords": ["amazon", "aliexpress", "shein", "temu", "jumia", "ebay", "zalando", "zara"], "category": "distracting"},
        {"name": "News", "keywords": ["bbc", "cnn", "news"], "category": "distracting"},
    ],
    # activity name -> category, set from the dashboard; wins over everything.
    "overrides": {},
}


def _merge_defaults(cfg):
    out = copy.deepcopy(DEFAULT_CONFIG)
    for key, value in cfg.items():
        if isinstance(value, dict) and isinstance(out.get(key), dict):
            out[key].update(value)
        else:
            out[key] = value
    return out


def load_config():
    with _lock:
        if not os.path.exists(CONFIG_PATH):
            save_config(DEFAULT_CONFIG)
            return copy.deepcopy(DEFAULT_CONFIG)
        try:
            with open(CONFIG_PATH, encoding="utf-8") as f:
                return _merge_defaults(json.load(f))
        except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError):
            return copy.deepcopy(DEFAULT_CONFIG)


def save_config(cfg):
    tmp = CONFIG_PATH + ".tmp"
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(cfg, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    os.replace(tmp, CONFIG_PATH)


def update_config(mutator):
    cfg = load_config()
    mutator(cfg)
    with _lock:
        save_config(cfg)
    return cfg


def _match_site(title, cfg):
    low = title.lower()
    for site in cfg["sites"]:
        if any(k in low for k in site["keywords"]):
            return site
    return None


def is_media(exe, title, cfg):
    if exe in BROWSERS:
        site = _match_site(title, cfg)
        return bool(site and site.get("media"))
    return exe in ("vlc.exe", "netflix.exe", "spotify.exe")


def _pretty_exe(exe):
    name = exe[:-4] if exe.endswith(".exe") else exe
    return name.replace("_", " ").replace("-", " ").title()


def classify(exe, title, cfg):
    """Return (activity, app, category)."""
    if exe in BROWSERS:
        app = BROWSERS[exe]
        site = _match_site(title, cfg)
        if site:
            activity, category = site["name"], site["category"]
        else:
            activity, category = "Web browsing", "neutral"
    elif exe in cfg["apps"]:
        app, category = cfg["apps"][exe]
        activity = app
    else:
        app = activity = _pretty_exe(exe)
        category = "neutral"
    category = cfg["overrides"].get(activity, category)
    return activity, app, category

lines.say: Apps are matched by their file name. code dot exe is VS Code, and it's productive.
Browsers are trickier, because chrome dot exe could be anything. So for browsers, it looks for keywords in the tab title instead.
These rules are saved in a config dot json file you can edit. And when you change a category in the dashboard, it's stored as an override, which wins over every rule.
Step three, analytics dot py, turns sessions into scores.
A deep-work block is twenty-five minutes or more of productive work. Interruptions under two minutes don't break it, so a quick glance at a message won't reset your streak.
The focus score is your productive time, plus forty percent of neutral time like email, divided by your total active time.
And here's how triggers are found. Every time a productive block is directly followed by a distracting one, that pair gets counted.
Step four, app dot py, ties it all together. It starts the tracker in the background, next to a small web server for the dashboard.
The server only listens on one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one. That address means this computer, so nobody else on your network can open your data.
Now let's run it. To try it with sample data first, add the demo flag.
Your browser opens the dashboard with three weeks of sample data, so you can explore every chart before tracking anything.
To track for real, run it without the flag.
I also packaged it as a Windows exe with PyInstaller, and put a shortcut in my Startup folder. Now it starts quietly every time I log in.

cards.text: A YouTube tutorial can be work. Set your own rules.

cards.title: Track a full week
cards.text: Habits show up as patterns, not in one day.

cards.title: Protect your peak hour
cards.text: Do your hardest task in your best focus hour.

cards.title: Break one loop at a time
cards.text: Pick your top trigger and replace it.

lines.say: A few tips to get real value from it.
First, fix the categories on day one. A YouTube tutorial can be work for you. One click in the dashboard sets it.
Second, track a full week before judging. Habits show up as patterns, not in a single day.
Third, find your peak focus hour, and protect it for your hardest task.
And fourth, break one loop at a time. Pick your top trigger, and when you feel the urge, stand up and stretch instead.
